> **Key takeaways**
> - Share good news often, and make it specific: what the child did, not just "great job".
> - Raise a concern in private and calmly: one observation, one plan, then a check-in date.
> - Never discuss a problem in front of the child or other parents.
> - Ask parents what helps their child. Describe what you see; never diagnose.
> - Keep your records short, dated and factual.

## Why these conversations matter

Parents can't see most of your class. They see drop-off, pick-up and whatever their child says in the car. What you tell them fills the gap. A short, honest word about their child builds trust, and it is often why a family comes back next term.

These talks can also go wrong. A quick comment at the door can sound like a verdict, and silence can feel like you don't notice their child. A few simple habits help. If keeping families is your goal, this pairs with our guide to [getting more students for your kids' classes](/blog/how-to-get-more-students-for-kids-classes).

## Share good news often, and make it specific

Most of your messages to parents should be good ones. If the only time a parent hears from you is when something is wrong, every message will feel like bad news.

Make the good news specific. "Great job today" is kind but forgettable. Compare it with:

- "Maya held her balance on the beam for the whole song today. Three weeks ago she needed a hand."
- "Ava finished her drawing and helped a younger child find the right colors."

Each one names what the child did, and often what changed. Aim to say something specific about every child at least once a term, more often for children who are new or finding it hard.

## How to raise a concern

Sooner or later you will need to share something harder. A calm, private talk usually works better than waiting.

**Pick the right moment.** Not at the door while other families listen, and never in front of the child. Ask for a few quiet minutes, or send a short message.

**Lead with something true and good.** Start with what you like about the child, and mean it.

**Share one observation, not a list.** Describe what you saw, in plain words. "In the last two classes, Sam left the circle during the warm-up and found it hard to come back" is clear. "Sam has a behavior problem" is a label, and it will put any parent on guard.

**Offer one plan.** "This week I'll give him a job during the warm-up, like handing out the mats. Can we talk again in two weeks?"

**Ask for their view.** "Do you see that at home too? Is there anything that helps?" Parents know their child far better than you do.

Then do what you said, and follow up on the date you named.

## When a child seems unhappy or isn't progressing

Sometimes a parent comes to you: their child doesn't want to come, or doesn't seem to be getting better. Listen first. Don't defend the class straight away. Ask "What does she say about class at home?" and "Is there a part she enjoys, or a part she dreads?"

Then share what you see in class, honestly. Progress is rarely a straight line, and many children stall for weeks before a jump. It is fair to say that, as long as you also have a plan: a smaller goal, a different role in the group, or more time on a skill they enjoy.

If the group truly isn't a good fit, say so kindly. A family that leaves on good terms often comes back, or sends a friend.

## Working with a child's needs, respectfully

Some children have needs their parents tell you about, and some you will notice yourself. Either way, your job is to describe and adapt, not to diagnose.

- **Ask the parent what helps.** "What works well for him at school or at home?" is one of the most useful questions you have.
- **Describe, don't label.** Say "she covers her ears when the music gets loud", not a guess at a condition.
- **Never suggest a diagnosis or treatment.** If a parent asks your opinion, share what you have seen in class and leave the rest to them.
- **Keep it private.** Share what a parent tells you only with staff who need it to run the class.

Small changes go a long way: a quieter spot, or a heads-up before a loud activity.

## End-of-term notes

A short note at the end of each term shows families you pay attention. Keep it to three parts:

1. **One thing the child did well,** with a real example.
2. **One thing they are working on,** framed as the next step.
3. **One idea for next term or for home,** if it fits.

Three or four sentences is plenty, in your own words. Don't copy the same note for every child.

## Phrases to use, and phrases to avoid

**Try these:**

- "I noticed that..."
- "Something that's working well is..."
- "Here's what I'm going to try."
- "Can we check in again in two weeks?"

**Avoid these:**

- "He's always..." or "She never..." (absolute words sound like a verdict)
- "He's the worst in the group" or any comparison with other children
- "I think she might have..." (a guess at a diagnosis)
- "Don't worry about it" (when a parent is worried, it dismisses them)

## Keep your records factual

Write short notes after class while it's fresh: the date, what you saw, and what you tried. "Joined the warm-up after a reminder" is a fact. "Lazy today" is an opinion, and it helps no one.

Good notes help you spot patterns, give accurate updates and hand a class to another instructor. Keep them where only your staff can see them.

## FAQ

### How often should I update parents on their child's progress?

Share something specific and positive with every family at least once a term, more often for new children or those finding it hard. Add a short end-of-term note. Raise concerns when they come up, not at the end of term.

### Should I talk to parents at pick-up?

Pick-up is fine for quick good news. For a concern, ask for a few private minutes or send a short message, so the child and other families don't overhear.

### What if a parent disagrees with what I've seen?

Listen and ask what they see at home. Children often act differently in different places, so both views can be true. Agree on one small thing to try.

### Can I tell a parent I think their child has a condition?

No. Describe what you see in class and ask what helps. A diagnosis is not an instructor's role, and a guess can upset a family and harm your relationship with them.
